summary:
Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes and waived a second vote. Its Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement reaches private premises as well as public buildings. IDEHPUCP recalls SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, in which a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where bathroom assignment was grounded on the sex recorded in the DNI. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement of the national restriction would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

National monitoring is the only violence data available for this territory. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020-2023, the homicide victims comprising 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. IDEHPUCP recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern is documented through single jurisdictions rather than nationwide reporting: the bathroom restriction originates in a complaint filed at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport, and the dismissal of a trans woman's complaint concerns a gym chain operating in major urban centres. Amazonas itself generates no legal or enforcement record in the sources, so the department's profile is an inference from national law rather than an observation of local practice.

Peru is one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, that lack LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, a comparative position that shapes what a trans visitor can expect from prosecution and redress.

Recorded violence is a floor rather than a measure. Killers went unidentified in 26 of 54 homicides between 2020 and 2023, and the state's crime-registration systems carry no sexual-orientation or gender-identity field, so incidents classified as ordinary homicide or robbery may conceal motive-driven attacks.

Regional monitoring by the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia is national in scope and does not disaggregate by department, leaving Amazonas without its own count of incidents against trans people.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains a long, costly and invasive process, and the sex recorded in the DNI continues to govern how institutions assign access to sex-segregated spaces, as the SmartFit resolution illustrates.

Since the April 2025 law, restroom entry in public facilities is determined by biological sex, and venues are barred from posting ambiguous or inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Residents face the same restriction as visitors, with narrow exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities.

In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, which affects how trans patients are treated and documented in healthcare settings.

Complaint routes have limited reach: a consumer-protection body dismissed a discrimination complaint brought by a trans woman against a gym, and hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such because sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from the state's crime-registration systems.

Article 4 of the April 2025 law bans media and advertising content under vague child-protection grounds, and the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years, constraining identity-related artistic, educational and journalistic work.
outOfScopeNotes:

The department's profile is derived entirely from the national framework, and local practice in Chachapoyas or elsewhere in the territory is not sourced.

Whether the April 2025 bathroom provision survived subsequent challenge or repeal cannot be confirmed from the available sources; the July 2025 ruling by a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree, but its bearing on Article 5.1 is unresolved here.

There are no Amazonas-level figures for homicides or rights violations against trans people, and no source disaggregates the national 2020-2023 totals by department.

The sub-registry caveat raised by Gianna Camacho about national hate-crime counts is unresolved: the true scale of violence against trans people in this territory is not established by any source reviewed.

Access to gender-affirming care, the presence of competent providers, and the practical availability of identity documents for visitors in Amazonas are not sourced and remain unverified.
